43: “He wanted to come and work in the vineyard today: father invited him,” she said, and after a short silence she fell asleep.
42: Maryánka dropped her hand on her folded beshmet , threw her arm over Ústenka’s shoulder, and shut her eyes.
41: “Oh, just chattering what came into his head,” answered Ústenka. “What does mine not say! Just as if he was possessed!”
40: “Do you know what he once told me: the lodger I mean?” she said, biting a bit of grass. “He said, ‘I’d like to be Lukáshka the Cossack, or your brother Lazútka—.’ What do you think he meant?”
39: Maryánka raised herself, and after thinking a moment, smiled.
38: “Don’t want happiness,” repeated Ústenka in a whisper, insistently. “But you are lucky, that you are! How they love you! You are so crusty, and yet they love you. Ah, if I were in your place I’d soon turn the lodger’s head! I noticed him when you were at our house. He was ready to eat you with his eyes. What things Grandad has given me! And yours they say is the richest of the Russians. His orderly says they have serfs of their own.”
37: “Hark at those young devils! Quite frisky! Not tired yet!” came the old woman’s sleepy voice from the wagon.
36: “Oh, leave off!” said Maryánka, screaming and laughing. “You’ve crushed Lazútka.”
34: Ústenka suddenly dropped her head on her friend’s breast, seized hold of her, and shook with smothered laughter. “You silly fool!” she exclaimed, quite out of breath. “You don’t want to be happy,” and she began tickling Maryánka.
33: “I do pity him, but I’ll have no nonsense. It is wrong.”
31: “Well, let him go to the others,” replied Maryánka proudly.
30: “A fine fellow! If he wanted her, no girl would refuse him.”
29: “Let him, indeed! Once I have said a thing I keep to it firm as a rock,” answered Maryánka seriously.
27: “Must you know everything?” said Maryánka laughing. “One night he came to my window tipsy, and asked me to let him in.”
26: “Just see what pitch! But you didn’t go, did you? And what a dare-devil he has become: the first among the braves. He makes merry out there in the army too! The other day our Kírka came home; he says: ‘What a horse Lukáshka’s got in exchange!’ But all the same I expect he frets after you. And what else did he say?”
25: “What should he say? He said he loved me. He kept asking me to come to the vineyards with him.”
24: “But what did he say to you?” Maryánka smiled.
23: “What has passed? A match was proposed. Father put it off for a year, but now it’s been settled and they’ll marry us in autumn.”
22: “Do tell me just this once what has passed between you and Lukáshka?”
21: “Well? Some who are married live happily. It makes no difference!” Maryánka replied quietly.
20: “Ah, Maryánka! When is one to have a good time if not while one’s still free? When I marry a Cossack I shall bear children and shall have cares. There now, when you get married to Lukáshka not even a thought of joy will enter your head: children will come, and work!”
16: “Now I’m a simple lass. I tell everybody. Why should I pretend?” said Ústenka, and her bright rosy face suddenly became pensive. “Whom do I hurt? I love him, that’s all about it.”
15: “He does. What of that?” said Maryánka with a sudden blush.
14: “Oh, you rogue of a girl!” said Ústenka, nudging her with her elbow and laughing. “Won’t tell anything. Does he come to you?”
10: But Ústenka kept on, “I say! But I wanted to tell you such a thing.” Maryánka raised herself on her elbow and arranged the kerchief which had slipped off.
9: “What humbug! Let me sleep. What have you come for?”
8: “Are you jealous?” asked Ústenka in a whisper.
7: And they both broke into such peals of laughter that Maryánka’s mother shouted to them to be quiet.
6: “Why, you’ve learnt it from Grandad,” said Maryánka, struggling. “Stop it!”
5: “Darling, sweetheart,” she kept repeating, between bursts of shrill, clear laughter.
4: When alone under the wagon with her friend, Ústenka suddenly put both her arms round her, and clinging close to her began kissing her cheeks and neck.
3: “Let me in,” she shouted to the little boy as she again crept under the wagon. “Is this the place for a Cossack—with the girls? Go away!”
2: She jumped up, plucked some green branches, and stuck them through the wheels on both sides of the wagon and hung her beshmet over them.
1: “Sleep, girls, sleep!” said Ústenka, making herself comfortable under the wagon. “Wait a bit,” she exclaimed, “this won’t do!”
0: Although there was no escape from the heat and the mosquitoes swarmed in the cool shadow of the wagons, and her little brother tossing about beside her kept pushing her, Maryánka having drawn her kerchief over her head was just falling asleep, when suddenly their neighbour Ústenka came running towards her and, diving under the wagon, lay down beside her.
